key.cite: Allen, G., Steene, R., Humann, P. & DeLoach, N. (2015). Reef Fish Identification – Tropical Pacific, 2nd ed. New World Publications. ISBN 978-1-878348-60-9

teach.name: Damselfish
cues: Tail from deeply forked to rounded
Most common family in IMR surveys

juv.note: Dascyllus juveniles: black with white blotches, still clearly Dascyllus. Chromis and Pomacentrus: no juvenile source found.

sub.name: Chromis
cues: Plankton feeders in large schools above the coral

teach.name: Butterflyfish
cues: Small terminal mouth: feeds on coral polyps
Dorsal, tail and anal fins curve into a disc
look: Angelfish: spine on the gill cover, iridescent blue

juv.note: Same disc shape; some Chaetodon juveniles add a rear dorsal black spot.

sub.name: Bannerfish
cues: No yellow on the saddle (Moorish idol has one)

teach.name: Angelfish
cues: Oval like a butterflyfish, continuous dorsal fin
Spine on the gill cover (opercular spine)
look: Butterflyfish: no opercular spine, no iridescent blue
phase: Juveniles look very different from adults

juv.note: Pomacanthus juveniles: striking patterns unlike the adults (e.g. dark blue with electric blue and white rings). Centropyge: no juvenile source found.

teach.name: Spadefish
cues: Black band over the eye in adults
phase: Juvenile and adult colours can differ completely
The juvenile pinnate spadefish mimics a toxic flatworm

juv.trait: very tall fins: greatly elongated dorsal and anal fins
juv.obs: They look much bigger than they are: very elongated dorsal and anal fins on a tiny body; as they grow, the body grows while the overall height hardly changes (Pierre, 2026-11-04)
juv.note: A resemblance to floating leaves or flatworms has been suggested, not established.

teach.name: Moorish Idol
cues: Only one species in the family
Yellow on the body and a yellow saddle
look: Bannerfish: no yellow on the saddle

juv.note: No source compares juvenile and adult colour; the horns are an adult feature.

teach.name: Surgeonfish & Unicornfish
cues: Scalpel on the tail base (caudal peduncle)
Moderate fishing vulnerability in the Philippines

juv.note: Acanthurus pyroferus juveniles resemble Centropyge pygmy angelfish (another family). Naso, Zebrasoma, Ctenochaetus: no juvenile issue retained or no source.

sub.name: Surgeonfish
cues: One scalpel on the tail base

sub.name: Unicornfish
cues: Two scalpels on the tail base

teach.name: Rabbitfish
cues: Slightly elongated mouth with puckered lips

juv.note: Juveniles look similar to the adults (Siganus puellus); same body plan.

teach.name: Parrotfish
cues: Swims with the pectoral fins, flapping like a bird
look: Wrasse: thick lips, no visible teeth
phase: Males colourful, females dark or dull
Intermediate and terminal phases look different

juv.note: Small juveniles are striped, alike across species, and change pattern as they grow.

teach.name: Wrasse
cues: Swims with the pectoral fins, flapping like a bird
Huge variety of sizes, shapes and colours

juv.note: Coris gaimard juveniles: red to orange with black-edged white saddles; Novaculichthys juveniles are unmistakable (a resemblance to drifting seaweed has been suggested). Most Halichoeres and Thalassoma juveniles look alike across species.

teach.name: Snapper
cues: Short distance from mouth to eye
look: Emperor: longer mouth-to-eye distance, deeper tail notch
Bream: shorter, rounder body, often a horizontal line

juv.note: Macolor juveniles: black and white pattern, very long pelvic fins. Lutjanus juveniles keep the snapper shape.

teach.name: Emperor
cues: Longer distance from mouth to eye
look: Snapper: short mouth-to-eye distance, shallow tail notch
Bream: shorter, rounder body, often a horizontal line

juv.note: Not very different from adults but not specific at all: early juveniles share a few patterns of stripes and bands, told apart by close examination.

teach.name: Bream
cues: Often a horizontal line along the body
look: Snapper: longer body, shallow tail notch
Emperor: longer body, deeper tail notch

juv.note: Scolopsis bilineata juveniles (black upper half with two yellow stripes) resemble the fangblenny Meiacanthus grammistes, another family. Other Scolopsis: no juvenile source found.

teach.name: Groupers
cues: Ambush predators that suck prey in
High fishing vulnerability: 3rd most exported fish in the Philippines

juv.note: Plectropomus laevis juveniles resemble the Blacksaddle Toby Canthigaster valentini, a pufferfish. Cephalopholis juveniles differ in colour but keep the body plan.

teach.name: Sweetlips
cues: Also called grunts: make sounds by rubbing their tooth plates
phase: Juveniles swim erratically to mimic toxic flatworms
Juvenile, sub-adult and adult look different

juv.trait: head-down, wriggling (undulating) swimming with exaggerated fin movements; bold creamy blotches
juv.note: A resemblance to flatworms or nudibranchs has been suggested, not established.

teach.name: Anthias
phase: Males and females differ in colour

juv.note: No source for the IMR species; for a related one, females and juveniles share one colour description.

teach.name: Boxfish
cues: Bony carapace: square, triangular or rounded
Swims with the dorsal, anal and pectoral fins; tail for bursts of speed
Releases a toxin when in danger

juv.note: Same box shape at all sizes; Ostracion cubicus juveniles are bright yellow with black spots.

teach.name: Goatfish
cues: Two barbels to search the sand for food
Feeds on invertebrates in the sand

juv.note: Barbels at all sizes.

teach.name: Triggerfish
cues: 3 dorsal spines that lock when threatened

teach.name: Pufferfish
cues: Sharp teeth crush invertebrates (crown-of-thorns, urchins, crabs)

juv.note: Arothron stellatus juveniles: orange with dark stripes breaking into spots, unlike the adult but clearly a puffer. Other Arothron and Canthigaster: no juvenile source found.
Thin source: Aluterus scriptus juveniles drift head-down with floating vegetation, offshore.

teach.name: Lionfish
cues: Long, feather-like dorsal and pectoral fins
Native to the Indo-Pacific, invasive in the Caribbean

juv.note: Same feathery fin plan; juveniles mostly translucent.

teach.name: Soldierfish
cues: Reddish body, big eyes; feeds at night
look: Cardinalfish: two widely spaced dorsal fins, small body

teach.name: Cardinalfish
cues: Reddish body, big eyes; feeds at night
First and second dorsal fins widely spaced
Rests still in reef holes or branching corals
look: Soldierfish: tall second dorsal fin, blunt snout

teach.name: Squirrelfish
cues: Reddish body, big eyes; feeds at night
look: Soldierfish: tall second dorsal fin, blunt snout
Cardinalfish: two widely spaced dorsal fins, small body

teach.name: Lizardfish
look: Sandperch: sits slouched, rounded mouth with thick lips

teach.name: Sandperch
look: Lizardfish: sits arched, triangular mouth with teeth

teach.name: Scorpionfishes
teach.why: scorpionfishes and Rhinopias (lionfishes are the IMR Lionfish entry)

teach.name: Garden eels
teach.why: spotted and spaghetti garden eels on the sand slopes

teach.name: Whale shark

wink.wrong: Bold choice. It's a whale shark, the biggest fish in the sea.

teach.note: A wink, not ID training: unmistakable and fun to meet (whale shark trips from Dauin).

teach.name: Thresher sharks

choices: Moorish idol (banner on the wrong end)
wink.right: Correct. That tail was a strong hint.
wink.wrong: Brave. It's a pelagic thresher: the tail is half the shark.

teach.note: A wink, not ID training: unmistakable and fun to meet (pelagic thresher, Malapascua).

species.name: Chaetodon baronessa
species.check: common name as in the PDF; probably Eastern triangular butterflyfish

species.name: Lutjanus russellii
species.check: common name as in the PDF; probably Russell’s snapper

species.name: Neoniphon argentus
species.check: spelling as in the PDF; WoRMS has Neoniphon argenteus
